tasks.intro: Here's an SQL query that selects data from a table.
tasks.notes: Use explicit column lists instead of `SELECT *` in production code so schema changes don't silently break your queries. Add LIMIT while exploring large tables.

languages.sql:
-- All columns (quick exploration only):
SELECT * FROM customers;

-- Specific columns, filtered and ordered:
SELECT id, name, email
FROM customers
WHERE country = 'US'
ORDER BY name ASC
LIMIT 100;

tasks.intro: Here's an SQL statement that inserts a row into a table.
tasks.notes: Column lists make the statement resilient to schema changes (adding a column won't break the insert). Use parameterized queries to avoid SQL injection — never concatenate user input into SQL strings.

languages.sql:
-- Insert one row (parameterized — never concatenate user input):
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, country)
VALUES (?, ?, ?);

-- Insert multiple rows:
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, country)
VALUES
    ('Alice', 'alice@example.com', 'US'),
    ('Bob',   'bob@example.com',   'UK');

-- MySQL / SQLite placeholder style is ?; PostgreSQL uses $1, $2, $3.

tasks.intro: Here's an SQL statement that updates existing rows.
tasks.notes: An UPDATE without a WHERE clause updates every row in the table. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to confirm which rows you're about to change.

languages.sql:
-- Always scope with WHERE!
UPDATE customers
SET email = 'new@example.com'
WHERE id = 42;

-- Update multiple columns:
UPDATE products
SET price = price * 1.1, updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE category = 'books';

tasks.intro: Here's an SQL statement that deletes rows from a table.
tasks.notes: A DELETE without a WHERE clause empties the table — always scope it with a WHERE and consider a transaction so you can roll back. Most production systems use soft deletes (a deleted_at flag) instead.

languages.sql:
-- Always scope with WHERE — a bare DELETE empties the table!
DELETE FROM customers
WHERE id = 42
  AND email = 'old@example.com';   -- double-check with SELECT first

-- Delete all rows but keep the table:
DELETE FROM customers;

tasks.intro: Here's an SQL query that joins two tables.
tasks.notes: INNER JOIN returns only matching rows; LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table, filling NULLs for non-matching right rows. Pick the join type by what you want to happen to unmatched rows.

languages.sql:
-- Orders with their customer names:
SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer, o.total
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY o.id;

-- LEFT JOIN keeps orders even when the customer was deleted:
SELECT o.id, c.name
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;

tasks.intro: Here's an SQL query that groups rows and computes an aggregate.
tasks.notes: Every column in the SELECT list that isn't wrapped in an aggregate function must appear in the GROUP BY clause — most SQL engines enforce this and error out if you forget.

languages.sql:
-- Count per group:
SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM customers
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY customer_count DESC;

-- Sum / average per group:
SELECT category, SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS avg_amount
FROM sales
GROUP BY category;

-- Groups with a minimum size (HAVING filters after grouping):
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM sales
GROUP BY category
HAVING n >= 10;

tasks.intro: Here's an SQL query that finds duplicate rows in a table.
tasks.notes: The HAVING clause filters groups after aggregation (WHERE filters before). Group by the columns that define what 'duplicate' means — grouping by every column finds exact-row duplicates; grouping by a key column finds records sharing that key.

languages.sql:
-- Find duplicate rows (same key, multiple entries):
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM customers
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- Delete duplicates, keeping one row per key (MySQL/PostgreSQL):
DELETE FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (
    SELECT MIN(id)
    FROM customers
    GROUP BY email
);

-- Same idea with a self-join (keeps the smallest id per key):
DELETE a
FROM customers a
JOIN customers b ON a.email = b.email AND a.id > b.id;

-- PostgreSQL row_number approach (keeps one per key):
DELETE FROM customers
WHERE id IN (
    SELECT id FROM (
        SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn
        FROM customers
    ) ranked
    WHERE rn > 1
);

tasks.intro: Here's an SQL statement that creates a table.
tasks.notes: Choose types carefully — changing them later requires an ALTER TABLE migration. PRIMARY KEY enforces uniqueness, NOT NULL rejects missing values, and a foreign key keeps related tables consistent.

languages.sql:
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,  -- MySQL: INT AUTO_INCREMENT
    name       TEXT    NOT NULL,                   -- MySQL: VARCHAR(255)
    email      TEXT    UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    country    TEXT    DEFAULT 'US',
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

tasks.intro: Here's an SQL query using an aggregate function.
tasks.notes: Aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) collapse many rows into one. COUNT(*) counts rows including NULLs; COUNT(col) counts only non-NULL values — a classic gotcha.

languages.sql:
SELECT
    COUNT(*)                 AS total_rows,
    COUNT(email)             AS emails_not_null,   -- ignores NULLs
    COUNT(DISTINCT country)  AS distinct_countries,
    SUM(amount)              AS total,
    AVG(amount)              AS average,
    MIN(amount)              AS min_amount,
    MAX(amount)              AS max_amount
FROM sales;
